concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Using a large pretrained model kind of works; it is not as clean as the hand-crafted model but works where the simple heuristic method was breaking, and future pretrained models are expected to improve.
concepts.content:
We learned that using a large pretrained model kind of works; it is not as clean as the results we had in the hand-crafted model section, but it works in situations where our simple heuristic method was breaking. We can expect performances of future pretrained models to keep improving.

With the hand-crafted model, we had a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms, assumptions, and limitations of our system. Another interesting advantage of the hand-crafted model is that it required no learning and no training data. Once the model was written down it was ready to work. It worked really well when the conditions were met, but it was fragile and unreliable as soon as we deviated from those conditions. Our hand-crafted model did not generalize outside the space defined by our assumptions. When the system failed, it was easy to point out exactly what went wrong with it, but knowing what was wrong did not help in making it work better.

Conversely, the pretrained system for 3D reconstruction seems to have generalized to our setting, at least to some degree, and it is able to deal with configurations that were not part of our modeling assumptions. The pretrained model is robust to changes in illumination and does not rely on fragile operations such as edge detection or figure-ground segmentation. But somehow, equivalent operations might be taking place inside the network. Information about 3D is still mostly contained in the edges, and information has to be propagated from the edges and junctions to the flat surfaces. How does the pretrained model work exactly? Has it learned some of the heuristics we introduced by hand, or is it using other ones?

[FIGURE:2d5b0345de81fa09 | A split-screen conceptual illustration comparing two computer vision paradigms. The left side represents a hand-crafted model with rigid, mechanical gears, cogs, and circuit-like lines on a light...]

GPT4-v seems to be capable of recognizing the geometric figures and their spatial configuration but the integration with the rendering engine seems fragile and was not able to create a new image with the same elements (although it is very close!). But why did it fail?

The precise answers to these questions do not matter right now. The field is evolving quickly and many of those problems will be addressed over time. What matters is that you should challenge existing approaches, and find what the relevant questions are for whatever new systems you encounter.

With learning-based systems we find ourselves doing experiments similar to the ones performed by psychophysics in trying to understand the mechanisms implemented by the human visual system.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of hand-crafted versus pretrained models helps us improve vision systems and guides us in addressing challenges in evolving AI technologies.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hand-crafted models require no training data and work well under strict assumptions but lack generalization.
- Pretrained models generalize better and handle variations like illumination but their internal workings are less transparent.
- Experimentation and questioning are key to advancing understanding and improving vision systems.

concepts.title: Parameter setting heuristics for recovering world coordinates
concepts.one_liner: To apply the world coordinate recovery equation, we set parameters $d_0=0$, $n_0=N/2$, $m_0=M/2$, $a=N$, and $	heta=\pi/4$ as heuristics.
concepts.content:
In order to apply the equation for recovering world coordinates, we need to define certain parameters: $d_0$, $n_0$, $m_0$, $a$, and $\theta$. Although these parameters could be determined using a calibration image, we opt for a simpler heuristic approach:

- $d_0$: Set to 0.

- $n_0$, $m_0$: Define the camera center point, where $n_0 = N/2$ and $m_0 = M/2$, with $N \times M$ as the input image size.

- $a$: Accounts for image size and camera focal length; a standard setting is $a = N$, where $N$ is the image width.

- $\theta$: Represents the angle between the optical camera axis and the ground plane. Although it could be estimated accurately by measuring the surface normal direction in pixels corresponding to the ground, we simply set $\theta = \pi / 4$, approximately the angle at which the pictures were taken.

Now we are ready to use the world coordinate recovery equation and the output.
concepts.motivation_md: Setting these parameters heuristically allows applying the world coordinate recovery without complex calibration, simplifying the 3D reconstruction process.
concepts.recap_md:
- Parameters $d_0$, $n_0$, $m_0$, $a$, and $\theta$ must be set to recover world coordinates.
- $d_0=0$, $n_0=N/2$, $m_0=M/2$, $a=N$, $\theta=\pi/4$ are heuristic choices.
- These simplify applying the recovery equation without calibration.

concepts.title: From 2D Images to 3D
concepts.one_liner: Apply a neural network to an input image to obtain disparity and transform it into world coordinates for 3D reconstruction without detecting edges or features.
concepts.content:
Let's start running the model on the same input image used as a running example in the simple system section. We apply the neural network to the input image, obtain the output disparity, and transform the disparity into world coordinates. We do not need to detect edges or other features computed previously; instead, the neural network has learned to compute whatever features it deems necessary to solve the task. We will not retrain the network using images from our simple visual world.

Just as before, to show that the algorithm for 3D interpretation gives reasonable results, we can re-render the inferred 3D structure from different viewpoints.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using a pretrained model. The images show multiple view points of the reconstructed 3D scene from @fig-simplesystem_revisited_img1)

It is remarkable that it works somewhat well even though this system was trained with natural images, which differ from our simple world. However, errors remain: the ground is not recovered as a flat surface but appears concave; cubes' edges are not straight and faces are twisted instead of flat.

We can compare this result with the 3D images recovered using the algorithm defined in the simple system section:

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)

While the learned-based model may lose accuracy in this example fitting our simple world assumptions, it gains robustness and generalization. The following figure compares results from MiDaS (learning-based) and the simple world model (hand-crafted).
concepts.motivation_md: This approach demonstrates how neural networks can infer 3D structure from 2D images without manual feature detection, enabling more robust and generalizable 3D reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Neural networks can infer disparity from 2D images without explicit feature detection.
- Disparity is transformed into world coordinates for 3D reconstruction.
- Learned models trade some accuracy for robustness and generalization.

concepts.title: A Simple Vision System---Revisited
concepts.one_liner: Hand-crafted vision systems produce beautiful results under ideal conditions but are fragile, while learning-based approaches yield good quality results more robustly.
concepts.content: When images fit the assumptions of the world model, the hand-crafted approach can produce beautiful results. However, it is very fragile; poor illumination can break edge detectors, causing a cascade of errors that propagate to the output. Conversely, the learning-based approach produces results of good (although never perfect) quality regardless of conditions. The hand-crafted approach completely fails even with small scene changes, such as changing the ground plane from white to black.
concepts.motivation_md: Comparing these approaches highlights the trade-off between accuracy under ideal conditions and robustness to real-world variability.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hand-crafted vision systems work well when assumptions hold.
- They are fragile and sensitive to illumination changes.
- Learning-based approaches are more robust but not perfect.

concepts.title: Large Language Model-based Scene Understanding
concepts.one_liner: GPT4-v interprets images by detecting edges, reasoning about perspective geometry, and estimating shapes, enabling accurate scene understanding.
concepts.content:
Another option is to use GPT4-v to interpret the scene. GPT4-v can take images as inputs and allows asking questions about them. The figure shows the result of asking GPT4-v to describe a simple world image.

This method is remarkably accurate. At one level, GPT4-v is a transformer trained on massive data using an autoregressive modeling objective. On another level, it detects edges in its first layers, uses filters acting like wavelets tiling Fourier space, and reasons about perspective geometry to find vanishing points and estimate shape, as discussed throughout this book.

(see figure: 3D reconstruction using the simple visual system from @sec-simplesystem)
concepts.motivation_md: Using GPT4-v leverages large-scale learned representations to understand and describe scenes accurately from images.
concepts.recap_md:
- GPT4-v can interpret images and answer questions about them.
- It detects edges and uses wavelet-like filters.
- It reasons about perspective geometry to estimate shapes.

concepts.title: unsolved solved computer vision problems
concepts.one_liner: Some computer vision problems seem solved but often are illusions; for every solved problem, many unsolved ones remain.
concepts.content: Computer vision is making amazing progress, but beware of the unsolved solved computer vision problems. For some vision tasks, it might appear as if one method perfectly resolves the task or that foundational problems are solved. It might seem impossible to make progress on certain questions. But more often than not, this is an illusion, and the solved problem was not really solved at all. Even when a problem was genuinely solved (and probably is not), remember that for every solved problem, many unsolved problems lurk in the background.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept reminds us to remain cautious about claims of solved problems and to recognize ongoing challenges in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Some vision problems appear solved but often are not.
- Progress can seem stalled but usually is not.
- Many unsolved problems remain behind solved ones.

concepts.title: A Simple Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: From a user's perspective, a neural network trained end-to-end for 3D perception is just a function call.
concepts.content:
When we introduced the simple world in chapter @sec-simplesystem, our goal was to recover the three-dimensional (3D) structure of the scene from a single image (@fig-simplesystem_revisited_img1).

(see figure: Image from the simple world.)

We derived an algorithm to recover the 3D scene structure from first principles: we started studying the image formation process, then reasoned where the information might be preserved, how to build a representation that makes the information explicit, and finally how to integrate all the evidence left in the image in order to recover the 3D information that was lost during the image formation process.

In this chapter, we will instead download a pretrained model that has been trained to solve the 3D perception problem from single images. The current state of the art is MiDaS @Ranftl2021, @Ranftl2022. The system is a neural network trained end-to-end using a diverse set of real images that had ground truth depth information and also using stereo images.

Maybe the neural net is not so simple, but at the end, from a user's perspective, it is just a function call. Before running the system out of the box, it is worth understanding how it was trained, what the output means, and how it can be adapted to our task.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding a pretrained neural network for 3D perception helps us apply it effectively and adapt its outputs to our needs.
concepts.recap_md:
- The goal is to recover 3D structure from a single image.
- Earlier, an algorithm was derived from first principles.
- Now, a pretrained neural network (MiDaS) solves this as a function call.

concepts.title: How Was It Trained?
concepts.one_liner: MiDaS was trained on a mix of four real-image datasets with ground-truth depth, using an invariant loss to handle scale and camera ambiguities.
concepts.content:
This model has been trained using a mix of four datasets with real images. The images below (@fig-examples_training_midas) show one sample from each dataset alongside their ground-truth depth.

(see figure: Images and depth maps from the training set. *Source*: Image from @Ranftl2022)

As the model is trained with a diverse collections of data sources, there is an ambiguity on the overall scale, camera parameters, and stereo baselines. Therefore, the loss is defined in a way that it can be invariant to all those ambiguities. The invariant loss makes the training more robust, but it also makes the output less convenient to use.
concepts.motivation_md: Training on diverse datasets with an invariant loss makes the model robust to scale and camera differences, improving generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- MiDaS trained on four diverse real-image datasets.
- Ground-truth depth was used for training.
- Loss is invariant to scale and camera parameter ambiguities.

concepts.title: Adapting the Output
concepts.one_liner: To convert MiDaS disparity output to world coordinates, invert disparity plus an unknown constant and apply camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: Converting disparity to world coordinates allows practical use of MiDaS outputs for 3D reconstruction by applying camera parameters and adjusting for unknown constants.
concepts.recap_md:
- MiDaS outputs disparity values up to an unknown constant $d_0$.
- Depth is computed as $z = 1/(d + d_0)$.
- World coordinates are recovered using camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters.

key_passage.text: MiDaS returns disparity values, up to an unknown constant ($d_0$), but what we need are world coordinates ($X,Y,Z$) for each pixel. To perform this transformation, we will use what we learned in chapter We will need to know the intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters and also decide the value of $d_0$.

concepts.title: Recover world coordinates from disparity
concepts.one_liner: World coordinates for a pixel are obtained by multiplying depth with the inverse camera matrix applied to pixel coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation provides a direct method to compute 3D world coordinates from disparity and camera parameters, essential for 3D scene reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth $z$ is computed as the inverse of disparity plus $d_0$.
- World coordinates $(X,Y,Z)$ are calculated by multiplying depth with $\mathbf{K}^{-1}$ applied to pixel coordinates.
- Assumes a pinhole camera model.

concepts.title: The intrinsic camera parameters (using perspective projection)
concepts.one_liner: The intrinsic camera parameters matrix $\mathbf{M}$ encodes focal length and principal point for perspective projection.
concepts.motivation_md: Intrinsic parameters define how a camera maps 3D points to 2D images, crucial for accurate 3D reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Intrinsic parameters matrix $\mathbf{M}$ includes focal length $a$ and principal point $(n_0,m_0)$.
- Used in perspective projection.
- Essential for converting image coordinates to camera coordinates.
